questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: An opening that closes a thread
questions.learningObjective: Identify an opening move that ends discussion instead of starting it
questions.stem: At a wetland survey briefing, a biologist opens by declaring that the sampling protocol debate is settled and that the group should now focus on logistics. Which description best captures what the opening did?

options.text: It closed a thread that was still open, by treating a contested point as already settled.
It redirected the group to a safer topic, which is a reasonable way to start a meeting.
options.misconception: assumes a redirect is always a legitimate opening move

options.text: It set an agenda, which helps a group of eight finish a two day survey on time.
options.misconception: confuses agenda setting with shutting down a thread

options.text: It invited agreement, since stating a position invites others to agree with it.
options.misconception: believes that stating a conclusion counts.

questions.explanation: A declaration of settlement removes the space for others to argue the point, so the thread closes on the terms of whoever spoke first. A redirect and an agenda treat the closure as something else.
questions.hint: Ask what opportunity the others were left to respond.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Repairing an opening that shuts a thread
questions.learningObjective: Explain how to reopen a thread that an opening closed
questions.stem: Explain how a survey team leader could reopen a protocol thread that was closed in the first minute of a briefing.

answer.exemplar: Reopening requires reversing the closure without pretending it never happened, so the leader would name the point as open, state what evidence would settle it, and ask a question that only the people with field observations can answer. Assigning it to the group rather than to a single reluctant participant protects the discussion from personal friction. The leader also has to accept that the reopened thread may change the protocol, because a repair that only collects views while the earlier closure still stands would be a different manoeuvre from reopening.

questions.explanation: A repair has to name the point as open again, name what would settle it, and invite the observations only the group holds. An apology alone changes nothing.
questions.hint: Ask what evidence would settle the reopened point.

options.text: The norm will hold, because the list makes the team's compliance visible to each other.
options.misconception: reads visibility of the list as proof the rule is followed

options.text: The norm is under-enforced, because no consequence follows a missed log entry.
The norm will hold, because a daily reminder is enough to establish a working habit.
options.misconception: believes frequency of reminder substitutes for consequence

options.text: The norm cannot be enforced, because photo logging happens in places without signal.
options.misconception: concludes a norm is unenforceable.

questions.explanation: A reminder and a list make completion visible but attach no cost to missing the rule. Visibility and habit formation describe the mechanism without showing what makes a norm hold.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a person who does not log photos.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Analyzing a redirect
questions.learningObjective: Analyse what a redirect does to a discussion besides changing its subject
questions.stem: Explain what a redirect does to the shape of a discussion apart from changing the subject being discussed.

answer.exemplar: A redirect also reallocates the floor, because the person who introduced the subject loses it and the person who redirected gains authority over what is now on the table. It changes what counts as a reasonable question going forward, since the unanswered concern becomes a thing the group has quietly agreed is out of bounds. It also shortens the agenda without anyone's agreement, so later items inherit whatever time the discarded thread would have taken, often compressed. The redirect is therefore a move about the group's permissions rather than only about its topic.

questions.explanation: A redirect also shifts the floor, defines which questions count, and shortens the agenda without agreement. It changes the group's permissions, not only its subject.
questions.hint: Ask who gained the floor and what became out of bounds.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a rotating role distributes
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a rotating role does and does not spread
questions.stem: Explain what a rotating role of writing the daily survey log distributes among the members of a field team.

answer.exemplar: Rotation distributes the practice of deciding what a day at the site actually contained, because whoever writes the log chooses which observations are recorded and which are passed over. Over several turns the members learn to judge significance for themselves, which is a capacity that a single permanent writer would have absorbed. It does not distribute accuracy of recall, since the underlying observations belong to whoever was present, and it does not distribute the load of the field days themselves. The rotation spreads judgement, not data and not hours.

questions.explanation: Rotation spreads the judgement of deciding what counts as worth recording, not the raw observations and not the total hours of fieldwork. Anyone present still owns the accuracy of what they saw.
questions.hint: Ask what the writer chooses and what the writer cannot.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: An opening that closes a thread
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an opening can shape the range of a discussion
questions.stem: Explain why the first minutes of a survey briefing determine which questions can be asked later.

answer.exemplar: The opening establishes what the group treats as a reasonable contribution, and later questions are judged against that standard rather than against the evidence. If the lead opens by treating one point as settled, anyone who disagrees has to argue against the room as well as against the facts, which most people will not do, so the thread dies quietly rather than being refused. If the lead opens by asking for observations, the group learns that a different view is expected and later questions arrive already framed as evidence. The minutes after the opening are largely a confirmation of what the opening licensed.

questions.explanation: The opening sets what counts as a reasonable contribution, so later questions are framed against that expectation rather than against evidence. A closure in the first minutes quietly ends threads.
questions.hint: Ask what the group learns about disagreeing.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A redirect that also silences
questions.learningObjective: Explain the silencing effect of a redirect on future contributions
questions.stem: Explain how a redirect that silences one question discourages later questions from the same member.

answer.exemplar: A silencing redirect teaches a lesson that is cheaper to obey than to resist, because the member who raised the question has just paid a small social cost for raising it while the group moved on. Once that cost is visible, the member learns that similar questions will be handled the same way, and the next relevant observation stays unmentioned. The loss compounds because the suppressed observations are exactly the field data the lead was waiting for. Silence after a redirect is therefore not consent but a rational response to the pattern, and it looks identical in the minutes.

questions.explanation: A silencing redirect teaches a lesson that is cheaper to obey than to resist, so the member withholds later observations. Silence after a redirect looks identical to agreement in the minutes.
questions.hint: Ask what the member learned the cost of speaking was.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What enforcing a norm requires
questions.learningObjective: Explain why visibility alone does not enforce a norm
questions.stem: Explain why making a field norm visible on a shared board does not by itself make people follow it.

answer.exemplar: Visibility informs but does not oblige, so a board tells the group what the rule is while leaving the cost of ignoring it at zero. Nothing happens to a capture that goes unlogged, so the person doing the logging is the only one who bears the effort, and under time pressure at a busy site the rule is the thing that gives way. A board also decays into background, so it stops being read after the first week, removing even the informational effect. Enforcement needs a cost or a checkpoint that would catch a violation while the data is still recoverable.

questions.explanation: Visibility informs but does not oblige, so the rule still costs nothing to break, and a board decays into background. Enforcement needs a cost or a checkpoint that catches the violation early.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the person who skips the rule.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Consensus where the record shows a split
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a summary can hide a split that the discussion contained
questions.stem: Explain how a written survey summary can record agreement on a point that the team never reached.

answer.exemplar: A summary compresses a long discussion into short propositions, and compression rewards whatever sounds settled. When a point drew two firm positions, the sentence that survives the cut is usually the one that reads most neutrally, and a neutral sentence about a contested point reads as a decision. Nobody has to intend deception, because the writer is usually reconstructing rather than transcribing, and the reconstruction smooths. The record then becomes a source that later readers trust, which spreads the invented agreement to anyone who quotes it as the team position.

questions.explanation: Compression favours sentences that sound settled. Unintentional smoothing then makes the invented agreement a source later readers trust.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to a two sided point when it is compressed.

questions.topic: A rotation that does not reach everyone
questions.learningObjective: Explain why informal rotations can exclude people without anyone deciding to
questions.stem: Explain how a rotating survey role can end up excluding a member without anyone making that decision.

answer.exemplar: Informal rotations are usually kept in someone's head or on a note in a pocket, and the rule that survives is the one that is easiest to apply. A member who is hard to reach, on a different schedule, or simply not present when the rota is written will find their turn quietly skipped, and the next person is offered it because they are there. Nobody chose to exclude anyone, because the skipping is a small convenience rather than a decision. The result is a rotation that looks open to everyone while covering only the people who are easiest to organise.

questions.explanation: Informal rotas survive the easiest rule to apply, so people who are hard to reach or absent lose turns to whoever is there. Exclusion accumulates as convenience rather than as a decision.
questions.hint: Ask who is easy to reach when the rota is made.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A redirect that also silences
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a redirect from a request for clarification
questions.stem: Explain how a request for clarification differs from a redirect in what it does to the discussion.

answer.exemplar: A request for clarification keeps the subject in place and asks the group to sharpen it, so the person who raised it learns that their question was taken seriously and the answer becomes more precise. A redirect moves the subject elsewhere and takes the raised question out of the discussion with it. The practical test is what happens to the original contribution: after a clarification the group returns to it and often answers it, while after a redirect the subject reappears later only if somebody with standing brings it back. One refines the thread, the other ends it.

questions.explanation: Clarification keeps the subject and sharpens it, so the raised question gets answered. A redirect moves the subject and takes the question out of the discussion, which is why it rarely returns.
questions.hint: Ask what happened to the original question afterwards.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Repairing an opening that shuts a thread
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a repair requires of the person who closed the thread
questions.stem: Explain what a person who closed a discussion thread must do to reopen it credibly.

answer.exemplar: The person who closed the thread has to undo their own act rather than merely invite others to speak, because the group calibrated to that closure. They need to state plainly that the point is open again, accept that their earlier framing was a decision rather than a neutral observation, and attach the reopening to something concrete such as a named piece of evidence to be checked. Silence in the room is the signal that the repair has failed, because it shows the group has accepted the closure and moved on. An apology alone changes nothing, since what the group needs is a change in what is now permitted.

questions.explanation: The person who closed the thread has to undo their own closure, state the point is open, and attach it to evidence. An apology alone leaves the group's calibration unchanged.
questions.hint: Ask what changed in what the group is allowed to say.

questions.topic: Analyzing a redirect

questions.stem: Explain how a redirect affects what a written record of a discussion will later show about the group's priorities.

answer.exemplar: A record lists the subjects that were taken up, so a redirected question leaves no trace of the concern that prompted it. The written record will show that fuel budgets and not methods were discussed, and a later reader will reasonably conclude that methods were not a priority, when in fact one person raised them and was moved off them. The effect is not only silence in the room, it is a durable misstatement of what the group cares about, which is then inherited by anyone who works from the record rather than from the participants. Redirects do not only lose threads, they rewrite the priority list of the team.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a rotating role distributes
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of a rotation on the organisation's knowledge
questions.stem: Explain why rotating a survey role spreads knowledge through an organisation better than appointing one expert does.

answer.exemplar: An appointed expert concentrates the capability in one person, which makes the organisation fragile, because the knowledge leaves when that person leaves and is unavailable when they are elsewhere. A rotation puts the practice into the hands of everyone in turn, so the capability becomes distributed and partly survives any individual departure. It also changes the content of the knowledge, since each holder brings their own observations into the role and the standard can be argued rather than inherited. The rotation therefore trades efficiency for resilience, and the trade is usually worth making for a capability the survey cannot do without.

questions.explanation: An appointed expert makes the organisation fragile and loses the capability when they leave. A rotation distributes the practice so it partly survives any departure.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the capability when one person is.

options.misconception: treats backup cover as the real failure

questions.explanation: A written rota is a plan, and practice can drift from it without anyone deciding, so a shared role consolidates with one member. Holding a turn once and backup cover describe other situations.
questions.hint: Ask whether the written plan and the practice still match.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A redirect that also silences
questions.learningObjective: Design a response that answers a question without redirecting
questions.stem: A biologist asks whether the ringing schedule could be shortened to allow more mist net time. Which response answers the question without shutting the thread?

options.text: Explain that ringing hours are set by the county recorder and move to the net schedule.
options.misconception: moves the subject to a decision taken elsewhere

options.text: Give the ringing and net hours the schedule currently allows and ask which the group would trade.
Note that ringing is a long standing commitment and that the group should not reopen it.
options.misconception: cites a standing commitment to end the question

options.text: Say the question is interesting and ask whether anyone has a view on the net hours.
options.misconception: defers the question to a general discussion

questions.explanation: Supplying the current hours and putting the trade to the group answers the question with information and keeps the decision with the people who own it. Referring to the recorder, ruling the topic out.
questions.hint: Answer with information and keep the decision with the.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Analyzing a redirect
questions.learningObjective: Analyse the aggregate effect of repeated redirects on a group
questions.stem: Stage one: over a debrief, three questions raised by junior members are redirected to later slots, while similar questions from the lead are answered directly. Stage two: what is the most likely cumulative effect?

options.text: The juniors will raise the same questions at the next debrief because the pattern was inconsistent.
options.misconception: expects consistency from an inconsistent pattern

options.text: The lead will be asked to chair the debriefs that follow.
options.misconception: reads the outcome as a succession problem

options.text: The juniors learn that raising a question is pointless.
The team will shorten the debrief by moving all detailed questions to later slots.
options.misconception: assumes deferring questions shortens every meeting

questions.explanation: Consistent differential treatment teaches the juniors that questions from them do not get answers. Repetition, succession, and agenda shortening each miss this learning effect.
questions.hint: Ask what the juniors conclude about the value of asking.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Consensus where the record shows a split
questions.learningObjective: Recognise when a record is an accurate report of a split
questions.stem: A survey record states: the team did not agree on the trigger for the second mist net session, with three members favouring a fixed interval and two favouring a humidity reading. Which judgement is best supported?

options.text: The record is misleading, because it mentions the disagreement at all.
options.misconception: treats naming a disagreement as itself a flaw

options.text: The record is incomplete, because it does not say which member held each position.
options.misconception: demands names where a count would serve

options.text: The record is misleading, because it describes the split as though the positions were even.
options.misconception: reads an uneven split as a misreported one

options.text: The record is accurate, because it names the disagreement, the positions, and their relative strength.

questions.explanation: Naming the disagreement, the positions held, and how many held each is exactly what an accurate record of a split looks like. Mentioning the split, needing individual names.
questions.hint: Ask whether a reader could reconstruct the disagreement.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: An opening that closes a thread
questions.learningObjective: Explain why openings that appear neutral still shape discussion
questions.stem: Explain why an opening that appears to say nothing about the subject still shapes what the group discusses afterwards.

answer.exemplar: An opening that merely sets the frame still tells the group what kind of contribution is welcome, and the group calibrates to it. Asking for observations invites contributions grounded in what people saw, and the discussion that follows stays in that register, so opinions and prior experience tend not to appear. Asking instead for decisions sets a different expectation, and the observations that would have justified them are never made. Silence on the subject is not neutrality, because every opening makes a proposal about the kind of talk the session will contain.

questions.explanation: Every opening proposes what kind of contribution is welcome, and the group calibrates to it, so a frame that looks empty still shapes what gets said. Silence on the subject is not neutrality.
questions.hint: Ask what kind of contribution the opening invites.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Repairing an opening that shuts a thread
questions.learningObjective: Choose the right moment for a repair

stimulus.body: A lead closed the thread about marking a small mammal grid by announcing that the grid would be fixed by the district officer. The grid marking is needed before the first trapping night in three days, and the district officer cannot be reached until the day before.

questions.stem: Given the note, which is the most useful timing for a repair?

options.text: Now, because the grid decision affects three days of preparation that has not started yet.
When the district officer becomes reachable, so the repair rests on the actual decision.
options.misconception: waits for the decision before repairing anything

options.text: At the end of the trip, after the grid has been marked and the traps set.
options.misconception: repairs after the work it affects is already done

options.text: Not at all, because the decision belongs to the district officer and cannot be reopened.
options.misconception: assumes the decision itself can be reopened

questions.explanation: Repairing now lets the team restart the marking work while it can still change the outcome. Waiting and accepting the closure lose that preparation.
questions.hint: Ask when a repair still changes the outcome.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What enforcing a norm requires
questions.learningObjective: Build a feedback loop that keeps a norm alive
questions.stem: One survey team wants its norm that every site is photographed at the same time each day to hold for the whole season. Which arrangement keeps it alive?

options.text: A written statement of the norm in the field handbook and a reminder at the start of the trip.
options.misconception: supplies a statement instead of a check

options.text: A fixed time slot in the daily schedule, a photo record with the time on it.
A discussion at the start of the season about why consistent timing matters for the data.
options.misconception: supplies the reason instead of a check

options.text: A request that the team try to keep to a consistent time when the weather allows.
options.misconception: supplies a request instead of a check

questions.explanation: A fixed slot makes the timing part of the plan, the timestamped photo makes it visible. A statement and a discussion rely on goodwill all season.
questions.hint: Combine a slot, a record, and a periodic check.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What a rotating role distributes
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate the trade-off a rotation makes in a survey team
questions.stem: Stage one: four members take a turn leading the acoustic survey. Stage two: which cost does the rotation accept?

options.text: A much higher error rate, since no member knows the method as well as the first one did.
options.misconception: overstates the cost of rotation to the whole team

options.text: A loss of any chance that the team will develop a standard approach at all.
options.misconception: predicts a loss of standards rather than consistency

options.text: Slightly more time spent on handover and slightly less consistency in how the survey is run.
The need to hire a specialist to run the survey instead of training the members.
options.misconception: assumes rotation means hiring an outside specialist

questions.explanation: A rotation buys distributed capability with a small and visible price, namely handover time and some variation in how the survey runs. Disasters, lost standards, and specialist hiring overstate it.
questions.hint: Ask what the team trades for the wider capability.
